topic: converting a bicycle into a cargo bike for a village bread delivery round

provenance.author: glowny-en-c
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a load and run plan for the same round with closed task questions, base is an advisory talk about choosing and fitting a delivery rack. Grounded external referent: the rack, introduced in turn 0 (the old one cracked at a weld) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (rating, mounting, loading, the steep lane).

a: The bread round needs a load plan, and the crate figures come first this morning.
Each crate weighs nine kilograms when loaded, and the rack carries four crates in a single run.
The round has twenty-two crates on the list for the standard Tuesday delivery.
Work out how many full runs that makes and also what the last run carries.
How many kilograms does the rack take on each of the full runs?
base: I deliver bread for a village bakery and my bike now has to carry the whole round.
The rack that came with the bike flexes badly when I strap two full crates on it.
On the last run a weld on the rack cracked and the crates slid into the hedge.
The frame itself feels sound, and the brakes are new from the spring service.
What should I look for in a rack that will take the round without complaint?

a: Twenty-two crates at four to a run makes five full runs and one short run.
The short run carries the last two crates on the rack at the end.
Each full run puts thirty-six kilograms on the rack at nine kilograms the crate.
The short run puts eighteen kilograms on the rack for the final leg.
Does the run count of six fit inside the morning window shown on the sheet?
base: Look for a rack rated for sixty kilograms that bolts to the frame at six points.
A rack that shares the seat stays and the dropouts spreads the crates' weight into the frame.
Welded joints should be smooth and even, because a lumpy weld is where cracks start.
Your cracked one almost certainly failed at a weld that was poor from the factory.
Does the frame have threaded eyelets near the dropouts, or only clamps around the tubes?

a: Now cost the fittings for the bike from the printed list the shop sent over today.
The rack comes in at one hundred twenty and the pair of side bags at eighty.
The stand comes in at forty and the light set at thirty on the same list.
Add the four lines together and give one figure for the whole conversion.
Which single line on that list costs the most money by itself?
base: There are threaded eyelets at the dropouts and a pair of bosses halfway up the seat stays.
The bike shop lists a steel rack rated for sixty kilograms with a wide flat deck.
The deck of that rack looks broad enough to take two crates side by side.
It costs more than I hoped, but the cracked one has made me careful.
Would steel over aluminium matter for a round that runs every day in all weather?

a: The rack at one hundred twenty is the biggest single line on the list.
The four lines add up to two hundred seventy for the whole conversion of the bike.
Next set the run times using twelve kilometres an hour as the riding speed.
Each loop is three kilometres of riding with ten minutes of loading at the door.
How many minutes of riding does one three kilometre loop take at that speed?
base: Steel matters here, since it bends and warns before it breaks, while aluminium cracks without notice.
A steel rack can also be brazed back together by any decent workshop in a day.
Two crates side by side sit best with the heavier one behind the axle line.
Fit the rack with thread lock on every bolt and check them again after the first week.
How steep is the worst climb on the round when the deck is fully loaded?

a: One correction has come through from the bakery before the plan is written up today.
Each crate weighs ten kilograms when loaded, not nine as the first sheet said.
Rework the load on the rack for a full run and for the short run.
The riding time of fifteen minutes a loop stands as already worked out.
What does a full run of four crates now put on the rack?
base: The worst climb is the lane up to the church, short but steep past the yard.
Loaded, I already walk it some mornings when the wind comes down the hill.
With a full rack I doubt I could hold the bars straight on that slope.
The gears go low enough, but my legs give out before the top gate.
Should the heavy crates ride at the front or the back when the lane climbs?

a: A full run of four crates now puts forty kilograms on the rack deck.
The short run of two crates now puts twenty kilograms on the same deck.
The riding time across six loops stays at ninety minutes for the whole round.
The loading time across six stops adds sixty minutes at ten minutes for each stop.
Does the round still finish inside the three hour window with those new figures?
base: Keep the weight low and central, and put the heavier crates in the side bags.
Bags that hang beside the wheel lower the balance point and calm the steering.
Save the deck of the rack for the light bulky loads like the roll trays.
On the church lane, a low load lets you stand on the pedals without the bars wandering.
Have you thought about walking that one lane and riding the rest of the round?

a: The riding takes ninety minutes and the loading sixty, so the round takes one hundred fifty.
The window is one hundred eighty minutes, which leaves thirty minutes of slack in hand.
Now add the second village, which brings six more crates to the Tuesday list.
Keep four crates to a run and rework the run count for twenty-eight crates.
How many full runs does the longer list make before the short run?
base: Walking the lane is honest advice, and the horse field gate makes a fair rest stop.
I tried the side bags from my touring days and they swallow a crate each.
The bakery wants to add a second village to the round from next month.
That adds six crates and one long hill that I have never ridden loaded.
Is there a sensible limit to what one bike and one rider should take on?

a: Twenty-eight crates at four to a run makes seven full runs and no short run.
The riding grows to one hundred five minutes across the seven loops in total.
The loading grows to seventy minutes at ten minutes for each of seven stops.
The round now takes one hundred seventy-five minutes against the same window.
Does the slack of five minutes meet the ten minute rule on the sheet?
base: The sensible limit is what you can brake, not what you can pedal up a hill.
Six more crates means either a second morning or a trailer behind the axle.
A small trailer takes two crates and follows without upsetting the steering much.
Keep the rack at four crates and let the trailer carry the overflow for the new village.
Would the bakery wear the cost of a trailer if it saves a second round?

a: The five minute slack fails the ten minute rule, so move one stop off Tuesday.
Shift the last stop of the new village onto the Thursday list instead.
That takes four crates off Tuesday and puts the run count back to six.
Rework the riding, the loading, and the slack for the shorter Tuesday round.
Write the final Tuesday figures on one line for the printed sheet.
base: The bakery will pay for a trailer if the round stays inside one morning.
I will keep the rack at four crates and hitch the trailer for the new village.
The wheel bearings and the tyres get checked at the shop before the first long Tuesday.
We agreed a trial week with the baker following the times on a printed sheet.
After that the round becomes mine alone, in any weather the valley offers.

a: The Tuesday line reads twenty-four crates, six runs, and ninety minutes of riding time.
The loading stands at sixty minutes and the whole round at one hundred fifty minutes.
The slack stands at thirty minutes, which clears the ten minute rule easily.
The Thursday list gains four crates and one extra run at the same working speeds.
The sheet closes with the conversion cost of two hundred seventy against the first quote.
base: A trial week is the right way in, and the printed sheet keeps everyone honest.
Watch the trailer hitch on the cobbles by the mill, where the shaking loosens pins.
Give the rack bolts one last turn on Friday and then trust the steel to do its work.
When the round runs quiet for a month, add the second village hill without fear.
A bike set up with patience will carry bread long after the van drivers give up.
